candidate.answerReason: The divisibility conditions force digits 2, 6, 5, and 4 into positions 2, 4, 5, and 6. The digits 1 and 3 can occupy the remaining positions in either order, and both resulting numbers satisfy every condition.

methods.label: Force the digit positions
methods.explanation:
Use the divisibility conditions to fix positions before counting arrangements. Write the six digits, in order, as \(a,b,c,d,e,f\), with each of \(1,2,3,4,5,6\) used once.

The five-digit prefix must be divisible by \(5\), so \(e=5\). The prefixes of lengths \(2,4,6\) must all be even, so \(b,d,f\) are the three even digits \(2,4,6\). Consequently, \(a,c\) are \(1,3\) in some order.

The three-digit prefix must be divisible by \(3\). Its digit sum is
\[
a+b+c=4+b.
\]
For \(b=2,4,6\), this sum is respectively \(6,8,10\). Only \(6\) is divisible by \(3\), so \(b=2\).

Now \(d,f\) are \(4,6\). Because \(100\) is divisible by \(4\), divisibility of the four-digit prefix by \(4\) depends only on its last two digits, \(c,d\). If \(d=4\), these would be \(14\) or \(34\), neither divisible by \(4\). If \(d=6\), they are \(16\) or \(36\), both divisible by \(4\). Thus \(d=6\) and \(f=4\).

The only remaining choice is the order of \(1\) and \(3\), giving
\[
123654\qquad\text{and}\qquad321654.
\]
Both work: their two-digit prefixes are even, their three-digit prefixes have digit sum \(6\), their four-digit prefixes end in \(36\) or \(16\), and their five-digit prefixes end in \(5\). Each full number is even with digit sum \(21\), so it is divisible by \(6\). The one-digit condition is automatic.

Every cute number was included in the deductions, and the two remaining orders give distinct numbers. Therefore there are \(\boxed{2}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
